name: Palazzo Imperiale
region: Liguria — Via Garibaldi (Strada Nuova), historic centre of Genoa
architectural_style: Late Renaissance palace by Giovanni Battista Castello ("il Bergamasco"); frescoes by Luca Cambiaso; part of the UNESCO Rolli system; still privately owned by the Imperiale family

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Palazzo Imperiale is accessible only through the guided Rolli Palaces tour — there is no independent walk-up access. Verify current tour schedule and available dates at the GYG listing or with the local guides.

visit_duration: 2.5 hours (combined tour covering all four Rolli palaces)
best_season: Year-round — interior palace visit, not weather-dependent; spring and autumn have fewer tourists in central Genoa
accessibility: Historic building with stairs. Verify current accessibility with the tour operator before booking.
tagline: A Luca Cambiaso-frescoed Renaissance palace that has never left its founding family's hands — still owned by the Imperiale family, 460 years after il Bergamasco built it
highlights: Built around 1560 by Giovanni Battista Castello ("il Bergamasco") for Gio Vincenzo Imperiale — one of three palaces in this Rolli tour designed by the same architect within a decade, a remarkable concentration of one master's work on a single street

Decorated with frescoes by Luca Cambiaso, one of the most important painters of the Genoese Renaissance, whose work helped define the visual character of the Republic's 16th-century Golden Century interiors

Registered in the Rolli — the Republic of Genoa's official Senate-decreed list of private residences fit to house visiting heads of state — from 1576 to 1664, across nearly nine decades of the system's operation

Sits at the end of Via Garibaldi, the "Strada Nuova" that gives the UNESCO World Heritage inscription its full name — a street that was itself a planned aristocratic showcase, laid out from scratch in the 1550s to house the Republic's elite
Still privately owned by the Imperiale family, the only one of the four palaces in this Rolli tour to have remained in its founding family's hands since the 16th century
description:
In the mid-16th century, the Republic of Genoa faced a problem that no other major Italian power had: it was one of the wealthiest commercial and financial forces in Europe, yet it had no royal court, no resident prince, and no single public palace capable of housing the visiting heads of state who sought its banking connections and naval resources. The Genoese solution was characteristically republican and bureaucratic — a Senate decree in 1576 creating the Palazzi dei Rolli, an official list of private noble residences judged worthy of hosting visiting dignitaries. When a state guest arrived, lots were drawn to determine which Rolli-registered family would receive them. Palazzo Imperiale was one of those houses — built some sixteen years before the decree itself, as if Gio Vincenzo Imperiale had anticipated the need.

The palace was constructed around 1560 by Giovanni Battista Castello, the architect known as "il Bergamasco" — the same master responsible for Palazzo Lomellino and Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino on the same street, all three built within a single decade on what was then a newly laid-out aristocratic showcase: the Via Garibaldi, then called the Strada Nuova. Castello's design follows the controlled language of Genoese Late Renaissance architecture — a restrained exterior that opens inward to frescoed rooms whose decoration carries the visual weight of the building.

That decorative programme was entrusted to Luca Cambiaso, the most important Genoese painter of the 16th century. Where Perin del Vaga, working at Villa del Principe for Andrea Doria a generation earlier, had brought the Roman High Renaissance to Genoa, Cambiaso developed a distinctly Ligurian visual character — a handling of light and form that eventually earned him a commission from Philip II of Spain for the El Escorial chapel ceiling. His frescoes at Palazzo Imperiale represent the defining expression of the Genoese Golden Century interior: technically sophisticated, tonally distinctive, and inseparable from the building's claim to represent the Republic at its zenith.

What makes Palazzo Imperiale singular among the four palaces on this Rolli tour is the thread of ownership that has never been cut. While Palazzo Rosso was bequeathed to the city, and the other Rolli palaces changed hands through marriage, inheritance, and institutional transfer, Palazzo Imperiale remains the property of the Imperiale family — the only one of the four to have stayed in its founding family's possession continuously since the 16th century. The guided tour enters a building that is simultaneously a historic monument and a working private property: a distinction that no amount of restoration can manufacture.
history: The Republic of Genoa reached the peak of its commercial and financial influence in the second half of the 16th century — a period its historians would call the "Golden Century" — as Genoese banking houses financed the Spanish Crown and merchants controlled much of the silver trade from the Americas. The Via Garibaldi, then known as the Strada Nuova, was planned from scratch in the 1550s as an aristocratic showcase for the republic's elite, its palaces designed by the best architects the city could commission. Gio Vincenzo Imperiale engaged Giovanni Battista Castello — "il Bergamasco" — to build his residence around 1560, then commissioned Luca Cambiaso to fresco the interior rooms in the years that followed. When the Republic's Senate created the Palazzi dei Rolli system in 1576, Palazzo Imperiale was registered in the official list, remaining there for nearly nine decades until 1664. The palace remained in Imperiale family hands through every subsequent upheaval — Genoese independence, French occupation, absorption into the Kingdom of Sardinia — and passed intact into the modern era. The UNESCO inscription of 2006, recognising the Rolli system as a whole, added an international designation to a building that had already accumulated five centuries of unbroken private history.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Palazzo Imperiale is on Via Garibaldi (also known as Strada Nuova) in central Genoa — a UNESCO World Heritage street walkable from Piazza Fontane Marose, Piazza Corvetto, and Genoa's main shopping streets. The nearest metro station is De Ferrari (~5 minutes' walk). The guided tour meets at a designated Via Garibaldi meeting point — confirm the exact address when booking.

**Tickets:** There is no independent walk-up access. The shared Rolli Palaces guided tour (t29705, from €15, 4.5★ / 593 reviews) — a 2.5-hour bilingual Italian/English tour covering all four palaces on this ticket: Palazzo Imperiale, Palazzo Rosso, Palazzo Lomellino, and Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino — is the only way to visit the interior. Book in advance; tour slots can fill on weekends and during Genoa's spring and autumn high seasons.

**Practical tips:** The tour runs for 2.5 hours and covers four palaces — the pacing is efficient but fairly dense. The bilingual Italian/English format means some explanations may feel slightly longer if you're only following one language. The street itself — Via Garibaldi — is worth walking slowly before or after the tour to appreciate the complete ensemble of Renaissance facades that earned the UNESCO inscription.

**Combine with:** [Villa del Principe](/castles/italy/villa-del-principe) (Andrea Doria's nearby waterfront palace — the only other Genoese palace currently on the site, built slightly earlier than the Via Garibaldi cluster for the Admiral who made Genoa a Hapsburg ally) and [Palazzo Lomellino](/castles/italy/palazzo-lomellino) and [Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino](/castles/italy/palazzo-tobia-pallavicino) — the other two Bergamasco-designed palaces on the same tour, both also on Via Garibaldi.

faqs.question: Who built Palazzo Imperiale?
faqs.answer: Gio Vincenzo Imperiale commissioned the palace around 1560, engaging the architect Giovanni Battista Castello — known as "il Bergamasco" — as designer. Castello was simultaneously at work on Palazzo Lomellino and Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino on the same street, making Palazzo Imperiale one of three Via Garibaldi palaces by the same architect built within a single decade. The frescoes inside were painted by Luca Cambiaso, the most important Genoese painter of the 16th century.

faqs.question: Can you visit Palazzo Imperiale independently?
faqs.answer: No — Palazzo Imperiale is a private residence and has no walk-up public access. The only way to visit the interior is through the guided Rolli Palaces tour (t29705), which also covers Palazzo Rosso, Palazzo Lomellino, and Palazzo Tobia Pallavicino over a 2.5-hour bilingual Italian/English circuit of Via Garibaldi.

faqs.question: Is Palazzo Imperiale still owned by the Imperiale family?
faqs.answer: Yes — continuously since the 16th century. It is the only one of the four palaces on this Rolli guided tour to have remained with its founding family without interruption. The other Via Garibaldi palaces were either bequeathed to the city (Palazzo Rosso, in 1874) or passed through multiple family lines and institutional owners in the centuries that followed.

faqs.question: What is the Rolli system?
faqs.answer: The Palazzi dei Rolli were a Senate-decreed list of Genoa's finest private noble residences, established in 1576 to solve a specific republican problem: the city had no royal court and no public palace capable of hosting visiting heads of state. When a dignitary arrived, the Senate drew lots to select which Rolli-registered family would host them — distributing the honor and the cost across the city's elite. The system operated from 1576 to 1664 and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006.
